newsitem.title: UK: Chilly answer to Major's terms dampens truce hopes.
newsitem.headline: Chilly answer to Major's terms dampens truce hopes.

text.p: Northern Irish republican leaders gave a chilly response to British Prime Minister John Major's conditions for allowing them into peace talks, dissipating hopes of an early Irish Republican Army ceasefire.

Major said on Thursday he was not prepared to negotiate with the IRA for a new truce but was eager to get its political arm Sinn Fein involved in the talks on the future of the province "as soon as possible".
The statement, made in response to proposals for a new IRA truce put to him by Sinn Fein and by moderate Catholic leader John Hume, was widely seen as a softening of Major's stance.
But republicans said Major was bowing to their Protestant Unionist rivals who want to maintain links with Britain.
Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams accused Major of sabotaging his and Hume's efforts to achieve a settlement.
"No matter how positively or softly Mr Major's statement is interpreted there is no doubt it is a rejection of our initiative," he said in a statement.
"Once again narrow party political interests are being put before the question of peace in Ireland," he added.
Sinn Fein has been barred from joining the talks, sponsored by Britain and Ireland, because the IRA last February abandoned a 17-month truce in its fight for a united Ireland.
Major's statement outlined his conditions for Sinn Fein's entry into the talks.
They were that the IRA must declare a "convincing and unequivocal" ceasefire, which Sinn Fein would verify in talks with British and Irish officials.
When the republicans could join the peace forum "depends on the words and deeds of the IRA and Sinn Fein," Major said.
But commentators seized on elements in the statement they said indicated Major may be easing the way for Sinn Fein.
Major did not demand a "permanent" ceasefire nor did he insist the IRA give up its arms before Sinn Fein was allowed into talks. "We are not seeking delay," he said.

He made reference to the Christmas recess in the talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell. This raised speculation that period might give the IRA and Sinn Fein time to convince Britain its truce was sincere.
But Hume was angry that Major had brought a sensitive debate out into the open: "I was rather astonished by today's events," he said.

He added he had sent his proposals to Major in early October but only received the response five days ago. He and Sinn Fein leader Adams met to discuss Major's stance on Wednesday night but had not yet had a chance to give their reply, he said. The Irish government, which had reportedly refused to sign Major's response to Hume, also issued a stern statement.

"The Irish government will not accept any exclusion of Sinn Fein once these conditions are fulfilled and hopes that when the talks resume in January, Sinn Fein will be in a position to participate in the talks, as a result, in the meantime, of an IRA ceasefire and of Sinn Fein having complied fully with the ground rules and the Mitchell principles," it said.
Major and Irish Prime Minister John Major are due to meet to discuss Northern Ireland on December 9.

Republicans believe Major is stalling over allowing them into talks because of pressure from their Protestant Unionist rivals. Major has a parliamentary majority of just one and often has to rely on the Unionists to vote with his government.
